idiom_name: SolidQueue queue tables + perform_later inside the business transaction
implementation_notes: Rails' default queue backend keeps jobs in the application database (solid_queue_jobs plus ready/scheduled/failed execution tables), so enqueueing inside the same transaction as the business write commits both or neither and the RDBMS is the durable store; workers claim rows with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, and failed executions stay in the database until they are retried or discarded. Retry policy is Active Job's (retry_on/discard_on) - Solid Queue itself deliberately adds none - and the job should carry a business id so a redelivery after a crash is idempotent. This is the idiomatic Ruby realization: the durable channel is a table, not a separate broker.
code_sketch:
class Order < ApplicationRecord
  def place!(payload)
    transaction do                       # state and enqueue commit together
      save!
      SendOrderJob.perform_later(id, payload)
    end
  end
end
class SendOrderJob < ApplicationJob
  retry_on Net::OpenTimeout, wait: :polynomially_longer, attempts: 10
  def perform(order_id, payload) = Gateway.deliver(order_id, payload)  # idempotent
end
pitfalls: Redis-backed Sidekiq is not a durable store unless Redis itself persists and is configured for it - enqueueing there is not guaranteed delivery, however reliable it feels in development.
Solid Queue performs no automatic retry: without Active Job's retry_on/discard_on, failures accumulate in solid_queue_failed_executions and are only visible in mission control.

A job enqueued inside a transaction that later rolls back would never run; keep enqueue and state in one transaction deliberately (or use enqueue_after_transaction_commit) rather than relying on accident.
Long-running jobs holding the same database as the app contend with web traffic; Solid Queue's own polling (SKIP LOCKED) needs the database to support row locking (Postgres/MySQL, not every adapter).

variants.name: Bunny publisher confirms with durable queues
variants.implementation_notes: With RabbitMQ the broker is the store: channel.confirm_select turns publishing into a confirmed operation, queue.publish(payload, persistent: true) marks the message persistent, and channel.wait_for_confirms returns only after the broker persisted it to a durable queue. Consumption uses queue.subscribe(manual_ack: true) and channel.ack(delivery_info.delivery_tag) after the business commit, with channel.prefetch bounding in-flight deliveries. Choose this over Solid Queue when other services (not just this Rails app) consume the channel or when the queue must outlive the application database.
variants.code_sketch:
conn = Bunny.new(automatically_recover: true); conn.start
ch = conn.create_channel
ch.confirm_select
q = ch.queue("orders", durable: true)            # survives broker restart
q.publish(payload, persistent: true, message_id: order_id)
raise "not persisted" unless ch.wait_for_confirms    # broker fsync'd it
q.subscribe(manual_ack: true) do |info, _props, body|
  save_order(body)                               # business commit
  ch.ack(info.delivery_tag)                      # then the delivery ack
end
pitfalls: persistent: true is ignored unless the queue is durable and the message is routed through a durable exchange; the half-configuration still loses messages on a broker restart.
Automatic connection recovery recreates topology but does not replay unconfirmed publishes - the application must re-publish messages it never saw confirmed.
manual_ack without an ack on every path (including exceptions) stalls the prefetch window and the consumer silently stops making progress.
A process killed between publish and confirm cannot know the outcome; a retry duplicates, so the consumer must dedup on message_id.
